scenario.name: Peer help marketplace
scenario.idea: A student-to-student marketplace where AI matches helpers to requests and payments go through the app.

advisor.summary: This marketplace handles location, payment, and message data from students who may be minors, and sends some of it to a third-party AI. The biggest risks are minors' data and safety, payment and message security, and unvalidated AI matching, so these should be settled before launch.

risks.severityWhy: Meets 'minors' data' and 'sensitive data' with no safeguard described.
risks.title: Minors' personal data collected without an age strategy
risks.why: You collect location, payments, and messages from users who may be under 18. Children's privacy rules at the federal level and in NC may apply, and parental consent or special handling may be involved. You did not say which ages you serve.
risks.fix: Decide the minimum age and add an age gate. If minors are allowed, build a parent/guardian consent flow and separate minor accounts with stricter defaults. Collect only the fields needed for matching and payment, and set a deletion schedule for messages and location history.

risks.severityWhy: Location data of possible minors creates potential direct physical harm.
risks.title: Location data could expose minors to real-world risk
risks.why: Precise location shared between students, or stored long-term, could enable stalking or unsafe in-person meetups. Collecting it may also be called out as an unfair practice if it is not clearly needed.
risks.fix: Use coarse location (campus or zone) for matching instead of GPS. Never show a user's location to other users. Make location opt-in, collect it only while the app is in use, and delete it quickly. Suggest public campus meeting spots, and offer virtual-only help options.

risks.severityWhy: Payment data and minors' data with no safeguards described.
risks.title: Payment data and breach readiness
risks.why: Payment info is a high-value target. If you hold personal information about NC residents, NC breach-notification duties may apply.
risks.fix: Never store card data yourself. Use a payments provider's hosted fields or tokens. Encrypt personal data at rest and in transit, restrict staff access, and turn on logging and MFA for admin accounts. Write a short breach response plan naming who decides, who notifies, and how.

risks.severityWhy: Minors' messages go to a third party with no safeguard described.
risks.title: Messages and personal data sent to a third-party AI API
risks.why: If user messages, locations, or payment details are sent to the model provider, you risk data leakage, unintended retention or training use by the vendor, and prompt injection from malicious message text. You also remain responsible for what you tell users about this.
risks.fix: Send the model only the minimum fields needed, such as skill tags and request category, and strip names, locations, and payment data. Use a vendor plan with no training on your data and short retention, under a signed data agreement. Treat message text as untrusted input and restrict what the model can trigger, such as payments or account changes. Disclose the vendor flow in your privacy notice.

risks.severityWhy: Plausibly applies: AI matching shapes who gets work and money, and needs mitigation before scaling.
risks.title: Matching may systematically favor or disadvantage some students
risks.why: Even though a human stays in the loop, rankings can reflect school, major, ratings history, or language patterns. These may disadvantage some groups and shape who earns money. Humans often defer to AI suggestions.
risks.fix: Don't use protected or proxy attributes as inputs. Log match outcomes and check for disparities across the groups you can lawfully measure. Give new helpers fair exposure, and let users see why a match was suggested and choose another. Document the intended use, affected people, and an owner for fixing problems.

risks.severityWhy: Plausibly applies: misleading claims about AI, vetting, or safety need mitigation before wider release.
risks.title: Deceptive-practice exposure from AI and safety claims
risks.why: Claims like 'verified helpers', 'safe', or 'smart matching', or an AI assistant that isn't clearly labeled, could be treated as misleading under federal or NC deceptive-practice rules.
risks.fix: Label AI-driven matching and any AI chat clearly. Only claim verification you actually perform, and describe what it covers. Keep evidence for performance claims, and make fees, refunds, and dispute steps visible before payment.

risks.severityWhy: Could cause direct harm to minors, and no safeguards are described.
risks.title: No described safety controls for minors messaging adults or each other
risks.why: A peer marketplace with private messages and in-person meetups can enable harassment, grooming, or off-platform payments. No listed source fits this, so check applicable child-safety and platform-liability rules with counsel.
risks.fix: Verify student status, for example with a school email. Limit messaging to in-app, with report and block buttons, keyword and AI-assisted flagging that humans review, and rate limits on new accounts. Block sharing of contact details before a booking. Set up an escalation path and a response time for safety reports.

risks.severityWhy: Plausibly applies and needs mitigation before scaling; depends on facts not given.
risks.title: Payments involving minors and holding funds
risks.why: Minors' ability to enter contracts and receive payouts, and whether holding or moving funds between users triggers financial-service rules, are open questions. No listed source covers this.
risks.fix: Use a payments platform built for marketplaces that handles identity checks and payouts, rather than holding funds yourself. Require a guardian-linked payment method for minors. Write clear terms covering refunds, disputes, and age limits.

askLawyer: Which federal and NC rules on children's and minors' data apply to us, and what consent or age-gating should we build?
Does our payment flow, especially with minor users, create money-transmission or contract-capacity issues, and how should we structure it?
What duties and liability do we have for user safety and for harmful messages or meetups arranged through the app?

plain.text:
# Risk Assessment: Student-to-Student AI Marketplace

The biggest risks come from combining **minors**, **location data**, **private messages**, and **payments** in a platform that connects strangers. Here they are by priority.

## 1. Physical safety and child protection (highest severity)
- **Grooming and predatory behavior:** Adults posing as students, or older students targeting younger ones. Location data plus private messaging raises the stakes.
- **In-person meetups:** Tutoring, errands, and rides can lead to unsafe one-on-one situations.
- **AI matching can amplify harm:** If the model pairs a minor with an unvetted helper, you are responsible for that pairing, even though a human makes the final call.
- **Mitigations:** Age and identity verification, background checks for older helpers, and restricting minors to matches within their age band. Use public or in-app-only interaction defaults, don't share precise location, and add guardian visibility, panic/report tools, and fast human escalation.

## 2. Child privacy and data law
- **COPPA (under 13):** Requires verifiable parental consent. Either block under-13s with real age gating or build full compliance.
- **FTC enforcement and teen privacy:** The FTC has been aggressive on kids' data, location data, and AI. Expect scrutiny of dark patterns and retention.
- **FERPA:** It applies if you integrate with schools or receive education records. Partnering with schools changes your obligations.
- **North Carolina law:** NC's Identity Theft Protection Act has breach notification requirements, and NC UDAP law covers unfair or deceptive practices. Check for newer state privacy or minors' online safety laws, since this area is changing fast.
- **Mitigations:** Data minimization, short retention, a clear privacy policy written for teens and parents, and a legal review before launch.

## 3. Third-party AI API risks
- **Sensitive data leaving your system:** Messages, location, and possibly payment context sent to a vendor may create COPPA/privacy issues.
- **Training and retention:** Confirm the vendor doesn't train on your data, and get zero-retention terms and a DPA.
- **Model errors:** Hallucinated or biased matches, inconsistent behavior after vendor model updates, outages, and price changes.
- **Prompt injection:** Users could manipulate messages or profiles to game matching or extract data.
- **Mitigations:** Send only the minimum fields (pseudonymized IDs, coarse location), keep payment data out of the AI path entirely, and add fallback logic and logging.

## 4. Payments and financial regulation
- **Money transmission:** Holding or moving funds between users may trigger state and federal licensing (NC money transmitter rules, FinCEN). Use a licensed processor with marketplace features (e.g., Stripe Connect) so you aren't the one holding funds.
- **Minors and contracts:** Minors can generally void contracts, and they often can't hold payment accounts. You'll need guardian-linked accounts.
- **Fraud and disputes:** Chargebacks, scams, off-platform payment steering, and stolen cards.
- **Tax reporting:** Helpers earning money may trigger 1099 obligations.
- **Mitigations:** Escrow-style flows via a processor, guardian-managed payment methods for minors, and dispute and refund policies.

## 5. Labor and legal liability
- **Child labor laws:** Paid work by minors is regulated, including NC youth employment rules. Some services (driving, childcare, certain physical work) are restricted or risky.
- **Worker classification:** Helpers might be seen as employees or contractors.
- **Platform liability:** If someone is hurt, plaintiffs will argue negligent matching and inadequate screening. Section 230 won't reliably shield your own AI's matching decisions.
- **Restricted services:** Ban categories like rides, alcohol, and anything illegal or dangerous.

## 6. Messaging and content moderation
- **Harassment, bullying, sexual content, and self-harm disclosures.**
- **Off-platform migration:** Users moving to other apps to evade safeguards or fees.
- **Monitoring tension:** Scanning minors' messages for safety is valuable but raises privacy and wiretap-consent concerns. Disclose it clearly.
- **Mitigations:** Automated and human moderation, in-app-only messaging, keyword and pattern detection for contact-info sharing, and mandatory reporting procedures (e.g., CSAM reporting to NCMEC).
